body:
## Problem

Nothing can react to a register being written.

## Current Workaround

Plugins that need to know when a register changed must poll `getreg()`.

## Solution

Add a `RegisterChanged` event. The pattern is the register name, and the payload
data is in `ev.data`.

### Example usage

```lua
vim.api.nvim_create_autocmd('RegisterChanged', {
  pattern = { 'a', 'b' },
  callback = function(ev)
    print(ev.data.regname, vim.inspect(ev.data.regcontents))
  end,
})
```

## Details

- Each written register fires only once per tick, using `aucmd_defer()`. A burst
  caused by something like `:g/foo/yank A` will only fire once.
- Covers registers `"a`-`"z`, `"0`-`"9`, `""`, `"-`, `"*`, `"+`, `"/`, `"=`,
  `":` and `".`. Does not cover `"_`, `"%` or `"#`.
- `RecordingLeave` fires after the register is filled, so `getreg()` in the
  handler returns the new macro.

---

Claude was used to write most of this code, but human-facing descriptions and
prose are painstakingly edited by me.

comment_data.body: adding a new, special-purpose structure is usually a red flag. there are already lots of "state holders", and the event system usually doesn't require a new one. maybe it's justified here, but it's the first thing i would try to iterate on and refine.
special-case functions instead of one central function `register_changed_capture` is a red flag
too much new, shared state. there must be a simpler way.
comment_data.diff_hunk:
@@ -998,6 +1057,491 @@ void free_register(yankreg_T *reg)
   *reg = (yankreg_T){ 0 };
 }
 
+// RegisterChanged
+//
+// The event reports net changes: it means "@x now reads differently", not "a
+// write happened". So a write is not an event on its own. Each write records
+// two things in a pending slot keyed by the register name - the value from
+// before the operation began, and the value it produced - and the slot is
+// drained at the next event-loop tick, where the two are compared and an event
+// is fired only if they differ.
+//
+// Deferring is what |dev-new-event| asks for, and it also makes a burst cheap:
+// further writes to a register that already has an undrained slot replace that
+// slot's payload instead of queueing a second event, so one all-in-one
+// operation produces one event per register it changed.
+
+/// Pending events, indexed by register name character.
+static RegChangedPending reg_pending[128] = { 0 };
+/// Whether a drain job is already on "deferred_events".
+static bool reg_pending_queued = false;
+/// Whether the drain job is running. Register writes made from a handler must
+/// not create new slots: a child-queue put extends the drain in progress, so a
+/// handler that writes a register would otherwise loop forever.
+static bool reg_draining = false;

comment_regular_data.body:
> human-facing descriptions and
> prose are painstakingly edited by me

That's appreciated, thank you. But the "Testing" section (at minimum) is an example of something that is never needed in the PR desc, it's total noise. Please be sure you read CONTRIBUTING.md

This is in Draft so I understand it's WIP, but my first impression is that it's way too much code/complexity.
@justinmk Thank you for the comments. I wasn't expecting a review so quickly for a draft PR! I am leaving town for the week, but I will review and revise the PR when I get back. Thanks 🫡

@justinmk Thanks for the review, and noted about too much complexity. I will move from `v:event` to `aucmd_defer()`. I also significantly shortened the PR description.

The reason behind the larger code section in `register.c` is that I wanted to coalesce multiple register changes into a single event. This took a lot of new code, but I think there's a compromise option available: remove the capturing of previous values and do not compare them with the new values. Instead, flag registers as "dirty" and emit the event on the next deferred tick.

If I do this, it means the event will fire once per tick for each register that was written, even if the value didn't actually change.

The name of the event might need to be different in that case, because it's not exactly "register changed," it's more "register written."

The "dirty" tracking would need a small amount of state (queue). Should that go in `autocmd.c` or `register.c`?

Questions:

- Is this a good compromise?
- What should the event be called? (perhaps `RegWrite` or `RegisterWrite`?)
- Would that queue be acceptable and if so, which file should it live in?
